lead: Sneaker collecting is a subculture built around rare, limited and vintage athletic shoes. Collectors, called sneakerheads, treat shoes as part of their style: footwear is often the anchor of an outfit, and a recognisable pair can signal taste and cultural knowledge.

The scene grew out of 1980s New York basketball and hip-hop culture and now has a global secondary market for resale. No studies have measured whether collecting changes how attractive a person looks, but the hobby is closely tied to fashion and personal presentation.

paras: Collectors follow release dates, called drops, and try to buy through brand apps, raffles and boutiques, or buy later on resale platforms. They build outfits around a pair, keep unworn pairs deadstock, and trade or sell pairs through consignment shops and online marketplaces. Many also share unboxings and collections online.

Rare pairs can sell for many times retail price, so the hobby can become costly. Counterfeits are widespread, which is why authentication services exist, and bots and resellers make popular releases hard to buy at retail. Some long-time collectors criticise profit-focused buyers.

angle.text: Collectors use sneakers as the centrepiece of what they wear. The hobby is about style and cultural signalling, so its effect on looks runs through clothing choice and outfit coordination.

lead: Sneaker collecting is the practice of buying, wearing, trading and displaying sneakers, especially rare, limited-edition and vintage models. Participants are known as sneakerheads [1][2].

For appearance, collectors use shoes as a main style element. Footwear sets the tone for an outfit, and well-known silhouettes such as the Air Jordan 1 or the Adidas Superstar carry cultural meaning that wearers use to express their taste [1][2]. Sneakers are also the most visible way many people dress up an otherwise casual look.
The culture developed in New York in the 1980s around basketball and hip-hop, expanded globally in the 1990s and 2000s, and now includes a large resale industry [1][2].
infobox: 1980s New York City, basketball and hip-hop [1][2]

paras: Rubber-soled athletic shoes date to the nineteenth century. The term sneaker is traced to 1887, when a Boston newspaper described boys' tennis shoes that way [1]. Keds appeared in 1916 and the Converse All Star in 1917 [1].

Collecting grew in the 1970s and 1980s. Street basketball players and hip-hop artists in New York popularised Adidas Superstars and Puma Suedes, and Run-DMC's 1986 song about Adidas led to a reported endorsement deal [1][2]. Nike released the Air Jordan line in 1985, which is widely seen as transforming the industry [1][2]. The scene went global in the late 1990s, with Japan developing a strong collecting culture [2].

The community uses its own terms: a drop is a release, a grail is a most-wanted pair, a colorway is a colour scheme and deadstock means unworn shoes [1][2]. Collectors cite childhood admiration of athletes and the nostalgia of finally affording shoes once out of reach as motivations [2]. Regional scenes differ, from California skateboarders adopting Air Jordan 1s to British casuals wearing Adidas styles [2].

Sneakers have some of the highest resale multiples among consumer goods, sometimes more than ten times retail for rare releases [2]. Consignment shops such as Flight Club (opened 2005) and platforms such as StockX and GOAT handle resale, and Nike's SNKRS app, launched in 2015, aimed to improve access to releases [2]. StockX reportedly sold 1.8 billion dollars of goods in 2020, mostly sneakers [2].

Long-time collectors have criticised resellers who buy only for profit rather than for appreciation of sneaker history, and the term hypebeast became derogatory by 2020 [2]. Bots and proxies have made popular releases difficult to buy for ordinary customers, and limited editions have fed a large counterfeit market [2].
